People like to blame immigration, overpopulation, and other things for bad jobs but the reality is that productivity per worker has skyrocketed in recent decades. Here is a graph of worker productivity from the St. Louis Fed. When one person can alone complete the work that previously required several you need an ever increasing amount of work to complete in order to maintain our traditional system of mass employment economics. And this is about to get very serious with the onset of automation. Not only does this mean there aren't as many jobs available (as a ratio to the population) regardless of the population, but the compensation for the jobs decreases since far more potential employees that employers means companies can, and increasingly many do, treat humans as disposable and replaceable resources.

Another negative is that bigger populations mean larger numbers of intellectual outliers - the people pushing humanity forward. People like Einstein, Hawking, even Elon Musk come from very unpredictable backgrounds. Einstein did terrible in school - dropping out of high school and initially failing to pass entrance exams for college only to end up working at a patent office after finally getting in and scraping by, Hawking was given 2 years to live - 50 years ago, Musk came from a single parent family in South Africa. You never know where greatness is going to come from and minimizing the population means even fewer opportunities for it to emerge.

Also I think as a species our general goal should be survival. Reducing the population would reduce our impact on the planet, but would also increase the chances of any given catastrophic event turning into an extinction level event. And the strain on immediate resources like water and food is grossly overstated. We can already desalinize ocean water and make it drinkable. The only barrier is money but the possibility of people in first world nations actually dying from lack of access to water becomes a thing those barriers would instantly dissolve. Similarly we're already generating enough food to feed billions more people than we already have and only using a fraction of all possible land for agriculture. We're also still relying on foodstuffs that are incredibly inefficient in terms of what's required to produce 1 unit of food. For instance cattle require hundreds of pounds of water/feed and enormous acreage of land per pound of food generated. Not only is there plenty more land to cultivate, but you can also get magnitudes more efficient production in terms of the consumables we produce if it came down to it.
